examined_directions.verdict:
This is the phenomenon's most natural frame and it returned exact-mechanism literature, but it neither fully explains the phenomenon nor leaves a bare void — it leaves a mechanism gap built on a challengeable premise.

The stated mechanism in this literature is proximity -> interaction: proximity raises the frequency of (informal) interaction and thereby ties. Reagans (2011) reports that teachers who took breaks at the same time or had classrooms on the same floor 'communicated more frequently and felt more emotionally attached'; Roche et al. (2024) attribute the proximity effect on knowledge spillovers to 'social interactions.' Network-evolution work explicitly names this the dominant 'interaction opportunities' logic (Kleinbaum, 2018).

What this literature does NOT cover — and, across the UTD24 set, appears to cover almost nowhere (the proximity x cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup query returns essentially zero on-point results; the only hit is a lab study of intergroup competition, Insko et al., 2013) — is the phenomenon's signature: the effect is boundary-selective. Losing co-location collapsed cross-functional ties while within-function ties stayed flat or rose, even though total interaction time was unchanged. A pure opportunity/volume mechanism predicts a general, roughly uniform decline in ties (every pair lost the same offices); the observation is a selective, boundary-aligned collapse, and the within-unit subset moved in the opposite direction (it rose).

This is not a void, because part of the literature already documents the phenomenon: Zuzul et al. (2025) find that COVID-era remote work raised communication-network modularity across 4,361 organizations, and Suh et al. (2011) find virtuality reshapes intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. So the literature does explain the phenomenon — but on an assumption worth challenging (see problematization_detail).

cited_evidence.title: Close Encounters: Analyzing how social similarity and propinquity contribute to strong network connections
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Frames propinquity's mechanism as increased communication frequency: teachers who took breaks at the same time or had classrooms on the same floor 'communicated more frequently and felt more emotionally attached'; propinquity amplified the effect of age similarity on tie strength.
cited_evidence.abstract: Models of network formation emphasize the importance of social similarity and propinquity in producing strong interpersonal connections. The positive effect each factor can have on tie strength has been documented across a number of studies, and yet we know surprisingly very little about how the two factors combine to produce strong ties. Being in close proximity could either amplify or dampen the positive effect that social similarity can have on tie strength. Data on tie strength among teachers working in five public schools were analyzed to shed light on this theoretical question. The empirical results indicate that teachers who were similar in age were more likely to be connected by a strong tie, especially teachers for whom age similarity was more likely to be salient. Moreover, teachers who took breaks at the same time or who had classrooms on the same floor communicated more frequently and felt more emotionally attached. Among the public school teachers, propinquity amplified the positive effect that age similarity had on tie strength. The strongest network connections occurred among age-similar teachers who had classrooms on the same floor. The empirical results illustrate the value of considering how social similarity and propinquity contribute to strong ties independently and when combined with each other.

cited_evidence.title: Proximate (Co-)Working: Knowledge Spillovers and Social Interactions
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Attributes the proximity effect to social interaction ('The main driver of the effect appears to be social interactions') and documents short spatial decay: start-ups more than 20 meters apart on the same floor are indistinguishable from those on different floors.
cited_evidence.abstract: We examine the influence of physical proximity on between-start-up knowledge spillovers at one of the largest technology coworking hubs in the United States. Relying on the exogenous assignment of office space to the hub's 251 start-ups, we find that proximity positively influences knowledge spillovers as proxied by the likelihood of adopting an upstream web technology already used by a peer start-up. This effect is largest for start-ups within close proximity of each other and quickly decays; start-ups more than 20 meters apart on the same floor are indistinguishable from start-ups on different floors. The main driver of the effect appears to be social interactions. Although start-ups in close proximity are most likely to participate in social coworking space events together, knowledge spillovers are greatest between start-ups that socialize but are dissimilar. Ultimately, start-ups that are embedded in environments that have neither too much nor too little diversity perform better but only if they socialize. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Funding: The authors acknowledge funding from the Kauffman Junior Faculty Fellowship and from the Harvard Business School Division of Research and Faculty Development. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.03555 .

cited_evidence.title: Microgeography and the direction of inventive activity
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Shows colocation raises the likelihood of NEW joint research 3.5x (driven by pairs with higher ex-ante search costs) but that 'separation does not negatively affect collaboration between previously colocated labs' — i.e., proximity governs the formation of new cross-cutting ties, not the survival of established ones.
cited_evidence.abstract: I provide novel empirical evidence grounded in an original theoretical framework to explain why colocation matters for the rate, direction, and quality of scientific collaboration. To address endogeneity concerns due to selection into colocation and matching, I exploit the constraints imposed on the spatial allocation of labs on the Jussieu campus of Paris by the removal of asbestos from its buildings. Consistent with search costs constituting a major friction to collaboration, colocation increases the likelihood of joint research by 3.5 times, an effect that is mostly driven by lab pairs that face higher search costs ex ante. Furthermore, separation does not negatively affect collaboration between previously colocated labs. However, while colocated labs grow increasingly similar in topics and literature cited, separated ones embark on less correlated research trajectories. cited_evidence.title: Networks, propinquity, and innovation in knowledge-intensive industries
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Treats physical proximity as altering 'the nature of information and resource flows through networks' — proximity as an opportunity structure whose effect is contingent on network position.
cited_evidence.abstract: Industrial districts and regional clusters depend on the networks that arise from reciprocal linkages among co-located organizations, while physical proximity among firms can alter the nature of information and resource flows through networks. We consider the joint effects of geographic propinquity and network position on organizational innovation using negative binomial count models of patenting activity for U.S.-based life science firms in industrial districts and regional clusters across a 12-year time period, 1988–1999. We find evidence that regional agglomeration and network centrality exert complementary, but contingent, influences on organizational innovation. Results show that in the high-velocity, research-intensive field of biotechnology, geographic and network positions have both independent and contingent effects on organizational innovation. The influence of centrality in local, physically co-located partner networks depends on the extent to which firms are also embedded in a global network comprising physically distant partners. Such global centrality, however, alters how proximity to two important classes of organization-other biotechnology firms and public sector research organizations, such as universities, research institutes, and teaching hospitals—influences innovation. Regional agglomeration shapes the character of information and resource flows through networks, while much of what makes industrial clusters region-like involves the structure of their internal networks. We conclude that network effects persist both independently and interdependently with geographic variables, and regional characteristics influence the degree to which centrality enhances innovation.

cited_evidence.title: Dynamic Silos: Increased Modularity and Decreased Stability in Intraorganizational Communication Networks During the COVID-19 Pandemic
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Directly documents the phenomenon at population scale: in 2020 organizations became more siloed (increased modularity) and 'once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community' — cross-subcommunity communication contracted while intra-subcommunity communication was retained.
cited_evidence.abstract: Workplace communications around the world were drastically altered by the COVID-19 pandemic, related work-from-home orders, and the rise of remote work. To understand these shifts, we analyzed aggregated, anonymized metadata from over 360 billion emails within 4,361 organizations worldwide. By comparing month-to-month and year-over-year metrics, we examined changes in network community structures over the 24 months before and after COVID-19. We also examined shifts across multiple communication media (email, instant message, video call, and calendaring software) within a single global organization and compared them with communications shifts that were driven by changes in formal organizational structure. We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. Collectively, our analyses indicate that following the onset of COVID-19, employees' communications began to shift more dynamically between subcommunities (teams, workgroups, or functional areas). At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos. We provide initial insights into the meaning and implications of dynamic silos for the future of work. This paper was accepted by Lamar Pierce, organizations. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02797 .

examined_directions.theory_name: Structural holes and brokerage (social capital theory of network structure)

TITLE-ABS-KEY(("structural holes" OR "bridging ties" OR brokerage) AND ("tie formation" OR "network evolution" OR "network change" OR "tie dissolution"))
examined_directions.verdict:
Abundant literature, but it is oriented the wrong way for this phenomenon. The brokerage/social-capital tradition treats network position — spanning structural holes — as an independent variable that predicts performance, innovation, and status (e.g., Zaheer & Soda, 2009, who further show spanning is associated with superior team performance). Even the strand that theorizes the 'origins of structural holes' explains spanning through prior status, centrality, and past cohesion, not through a physical co-location shock (Zaheer & Soda, 2009). 

Consequently this direction names the phenomenon's outcome (fewer bridging ties = lost structural holes) but does not supply the mechanism by which an entire organization's loss of co-location selectively dismantles bridging ties. It is downstream of the propinquity direction and produces no independent puzzle.

cited_evidence.title: Network evolution: The origins of structural holes
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Theorizes the emergence of bridging position as a function of 'structural constraints and network opportunities' — prior status/centrality and past cohesion — and links spanning to performance, i.e., network structure is treated as an independent variable, not as a dependent variable responding to co-location loss.
cited_evidence.abstract: We develop and test a theory of the origins of network structures, specifically of structural holes, building and testing a theoretical framework proposing that network structures emerge from the interplay of two complementary forces: structural constraints and network opportunities. We analyze data on a co-membership network among 501 production teams in the Italian TV production industry tracked over a period of 12 years, explicitly accounting for endogeneity. We find that structural holes spanned by teams originate from the prior status and centrality of teams that members were part of in the past, in addition to structural holes spanned in the past. But a focal team spans fewer structural holes if its members were part of cohesive teams earlier and if the past teams they were connected to produced similar artistic content. We also demonstrate that spanning structural holes is associated with superior team performance in terms of greater viewership. The results support both opportunity exploitation and structural constraint explanations, although we find that homogeneity rather than diversity influences performance across structural holes.

examined_directions.theory_name: Boundary spanning and cross-boundary coordination in organizations
queries_tried: TITLE-ABS-KEY("boundary spanning" AND (coordination OR "cross-functional" OR organization OR team))
examined_directions.verdict: Rich, on-topic literature, but its dependent variable is boundary-spanning behavior, role/practice, and its performance consequences — not the network of who is connected to whom. Kellogg et al. (2006) theorize cross-boundary 'trading zone' coordination practices, and Marrone et al. (2007) examine antecedents and the role-overload paradox of boundary-spanning individuals. Both presuppose that cross-boundary interaction exists and ask how it is performed and coordinated; neither theorizes how physical co-location enables or disables boundary-spanning ties in the first place. This direction therefore describes the coordination activity that collapsed but does not explain why co-location loss selectively severed it, and it overlaps with the propinquity direction. No independent puzzle.

cited_evidence.title: Life in the trading zone: Structuring coordination across boundaries in postbureaucratic organizations
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Examines how members of different communities 'perform boundary-spanning coordination work' through visibility/legibility practices — the focus is on coordination practices and structures, taking cross-boundary interaction as given rather than theorizing its spatial enabling conditions.
cited_evidence.abstract: In our study of an interactive marketing organization, we examine how members of different communities perform boundary-spanning coordination work in conditions of high speed, uncertainty, and rapid change. We find that members engage in a number of cross-boundary coordination practices that make their work visible and legible to each other, and that enable ongoing revision and alignment. Drawing on the notion of a "trading zone," we suggest that by engaging in these practices, members enact a coordination structure that affords cross-boundary coordination while facilitating adaptability, speed, and learning. We also find that these coordination practices do not eliminate jurisdictional conflicts, and often generate problematic consequences such as the privileging of speed over quality, suppression of difference, loss of comprehension, misinterpretation and ambiguity, rework, and temporal pressure. After discussing our empirical findings, we explore their implications for organizations attempting to operate in the uncertain and rapidly changing contexts of postbureaucratic work.

cited_evidence.title: A multilevel investigation of antecedents and consequences of team member boundary-spanning behavior
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Focuses on antecedents of individual boundary-spanning behavior and its role-overload/viability consequences (the 'boundary-spanning paradox') — not on how loss of co-location removes the conditions for boundary-spanning ties.
cited_evidence.abstract: We adopt a multilevel approach to a paradox that arises when research findings on the performance benefits of team boundary spanning are juxtaposed with earlier work demonstrating the role overload of individuals who span boundaries. Results revealed that individual and team-level factors predicted member boundary-spanning behavior, which increases individual role overload, which then negatively impacts team viability. However, when we aggregated to the team level of analysis, higher levels of boundary spanning resulted in team members' experiencing significantly less role overload. Implications for addressing the boundary-spanning paradox and developing a multilevel theory of team boundary spanning are discussed.

examined_directions.theory_name: Media synchronicity theory / computer-mediated communication (face-to-face vs digital channels)
queries_tried: TITLE-ABS-KEY("media synchronicity" AND (communication OR team OR "task performance"))
TITLE-ABS-KEY(("computer-mediated communication" OR "virtuality" OR "electronic communication") AND (team OR organization) AND (performance OR coordination OR "social network"))
examined_directions.verdict: Media synchronicity theory (Dennis et al., 2008) explains how media capabilities support the conveyance/convergence processes of task communication, and CMC/'virtuality' work shows digital channels can partly substitute for face-to-face interaction (Suh et al., 2011). Its dependent variable, however, is the quality/success of communication for a task, not the boundary-selective reshaping of the tie network. Because the phenomenon's total meeting time and logged hours were preserved, it is not a story about lost communication volume or a synchronicity deficit; what changed is who is connected to whom. This direction is adjacent but does not carry the puzzle.

cited_evidence.title: Media, tasks, and communication processes: A theory of media synchronicity
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: MST's dependent variable is communication performance for conveyance/convergence processes as a function of media capabilities — it does not address the composition of an organization's tie network or boundary-crossing connectivity.
cited_evidence.abstract: This paper expands, refines, and explicates media synchronicity theory, originally proposed in a conference proceeding in 1999 (Dennis and Valacich 1999). Media synchronicity theory (MST) focuses on the ability of media to support synchronicity, a shared pattern of coordinated behavior among individuals as they work together. We expand on the original propositions of MST to argue that communication is composed of two primary processes: conveyance and convergence. The familiarity of individuals with the tasks they are performing and with their coworkers will also affect the relative amounts of these two processes. Media synchronicity theory proposes that for conveyance processes, use of media supporting lower synchronicity should result in better communication performance. For convergence processes, use of media supporting higher synchronicity should result in better communication performance. We identify five capabilities of media (symbol sets, parallelism, transmission velocity, rehearsability, and reprocessability) that influence the development of synchronicity and thus the successful performance of conveyance and convergence communication processes. The successful completion of most tasks involving more than one individual requires both conveyance and convergence processes, thus communication performance will be improved when individuals use a variety of media to perform a task, rather than just one medium.

research_question: Why does removing physical co-location from an entire organization's workforce — while total logged working hours and meeting time are preserved — selectively collapse ties that cross functional boundaries while leaving ties within functional units intact or strengthened? And does this imply that physical proximity governs the *composition* of organizational interaction (which boundaries are crossed) rather than its *volume*?

assumption_evidence.title: Reorganization and tie decay choices
assumption_evidence.relevant_snippet: States the dominant premise explicitly and pivots away from it: 'most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices' — i.e., the field is assumed to run on interaction opportunity.
assumption_evidence.abstract: Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. I argue that, conditional on changes in opportunity, people (especially those with Machiavellian personalities) choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties (especially with highly empathic others), and they retain socially embedded ties (especially if they are low self-monitors). The empirical design, which exploits a randomized natural experiment, confirms these hypotheses and suggests that our understanding of tie decay choices—and, consequently, of network evolution—is enhanced by an integrated theoretical perspective that encompasses both social structure and social psychology. This paper was accepted by Olav Sorenson, organizations.

problematization_detail.why_worth_challenging: The assumption is broadly shared but weakly argued on its own terms: papers report proximity -> interaction-frequency correlations and conclude that interaction mediates the proximity-tie link, without testing whether the *amount* of interaction, rather than its *composition*, is doing the work. It is also visibly starting to lose explanatory power from within: Kleinbaum (2018) explicitly pivots from 'interaction opportunities' to 'tie decay choices,' and Catalini (2018) finds that separation does not reduce collaboration among previously colocated labs. Most importantly, the phenomenon card puts the assumption in direct tension: total logged working hours and meeting time were almost identical before and after the shift, so the realized amount of interaction did not change — yet cross-functional ties collapsed sharply. If the network's connectivity were a function of interaction quantity, no such collapse should appear.
problematization_detail.alternative_assumption: Physical co-location does not govern how much organizational interaction occurs, but who is exposed to whom — it functions as a boundary-crossing exposure/search mechanism that seeds novel, cross-boundary ties, while within-boundary ties are sustained by shared task structure and unit membership without requiring proximity. On this reading, interaction volume and network composition are decoupled: an organization can hold total interaction time constant while its cross-boundary connectivity collapses. (Constructed from the retrieved literature: Catalini, 2018, shows colocation raises the formation of new cross-cutting collaborations by 3.5x while separation leaves previously colocated labs' collaboration intact but makes separated labs' research trajectories less correlated; Chai and Freeman, 2019, show temporary colocation mainly enables collaborations between researchers with no prior ties.)
problematization_detail.interestingness_check: That's interesting. The alternative partly affirms what the audience already assumes (physical proximity genuinely matters for cross-boundary connectivity) and partly overturns it (proximity does not operate through, and is not indexed by, the amount of interaction — network breadth can decouple from the interaction base). It is not 'obvious,' because it directly negates the frequency/opportunity mechanism statements the literature actually relies on (Reagans, 2011; Roche et al., 2024); it is not 'absurd,' because it retains proximity's causal role and only relocates it from volume to composition. Honest caveat: a reader could deflate it to the familiar 'proximity shapes who you meet,' which is why the load-bearing claim in the research question is the decoupling of interaction volume from cross-boundary connectivity, not the bare claim that proximity matters for ties.

coverage_report:
Searches were run on all four candidate directions before settling; the retrieval trail is recorded in each direction's `queries_tried`.

1. **Propinquity / physical proximity theory** (examined first): reached the exact-mechanism level. On-point hits include Reagans (2011), Roche et al. (2024), Catalini (2018), Chai and Freeman (2019), Whittington et al. (2009), Kleinbaum (2018), plus the COVID/remote-work networking work of Zuzul et al. (2025), Suh et al. (2011), Wu et al. (2021), and Kneeland and Kleinbaum (2025). Critically, the targeted query pairing proximity with cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup tie types returns essentially nothing relevant (only a lab study of intergroup competition, Insko et al., 2013), showing the boundary-selective framing is not covered in this literature.

2. **Structural holes and brokerage**: reached the theory-family level (137 hits). Retrieved Zaheer and Soda (2009), Ahuja (2000), Shipilov et al. (2023), Soda et al. (2018), among others. The literature treats spanning as an independent variable for performance, not as a dependent variable responding to co-location loss.

3. **Boundary spanning / cross-boundary coordination**: reached the theory-family level (61 hits). Retrieved Kellogg et al. (2006), Marrone et al. (2007), Faraj and Yan (2009), De Vries et al. (2014), Ziegert et al. (2022). Focus is on boundary-spanning behavior and coordination practices, presupposing cross-boundary interaction.

4. **Media synchronicity / CMC**: reached the theory-family level. Retrieved Dennis et al. (2008), Robert et al. (2018), Tenzer et al. (2016), Gajendran et al. (2022), Suh et al. (2011), Mesmer-Magnus et al. (2011). Concerned with media-capability fit for task communication, not tie-network composition.

Direction 1 was selected as the anchor and received an additional narrow-and-deep pass (see `anchor_theory_grounding`).
rationale:
The four directions were examined in the given order. Direction 1 (propinquity) returned exact-mechanism literature and was selected as the anchor; directions 2-4 returned substantial but miss-oriented literature and were judged not to carry the puzzle (recorded above).

**Why direction 1 does not simply "fully explain" the phenomenon.** Part of this literature does document the phenomenon at scale — Zuzul et al. (2025) find remote work raised communication-network modularity across 4,361 organizations, and Suh et al. (2011) show virtuality reshapes intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. But the specific signature of this phenomenon is not covered: the effect is *boundary-selective*. Losing co-location collapsed cross-functional ties while within-function ties stayed flat or rose, with total logged hours and meeting time unchanged. A targeted search pairing proximity with cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup ties yields essentially no on-point work, so the boundary-selective outcome variable is genuinely unaddressed.

**Why problematization rather than gap-spotting.** Applying both lenses to the retrieved literature: the dominant stated mechanism is proximity -> interaction (Reagans, 2011; Roche et al., 2024), and network-evolution work names this the "interaction opportunities" logic (Kleinbaum, 2018). That makes the direction more than a void — the literature *does* explain the phenomenon, but on an assumption (proximity operates through the amount/opportunity of interaction) that the phenomenon's "unchanged totals" sits in direct tension with. Per the A&S guidance, when a problematization and a gap-spotting outcome both hold, problematization is preferred. Critically, this is not a forced or "prepackaged" problematization: the alternative assumption is constructed from the retrieved literature itself (Catalini, 2018, finds separation does *not* reduce collaboration between previously colocated labs, and that colocation instead drives new cross-cutting research trajectories; Chai and Freeman, 2019, find temporary colocation primarily enables collaborations between researchers with *no prior* ties), i.e., it points toward a composition/search reading rather than a volume reading. The alternative assumption passes Davis's three-way test (it partly affirms that proximity matters while denying the volume-mediator premise).

**Why not the safer mechanism_gap/anomalous_reversal framing.** A gap-spotting reading is defensible (one could argue the theory's opportunity logic predicts a general decline while the observation is a selective one — an anomalous reversal for the within-unit subset). I preferred problematization because the literature already documents the phenomenon, making "it covers it, but on a challengeable assumption" a more accurate characterization than "its mechanism doesn't cover this part." An honest caveat: the alternative assumption risks reading as obvious if collapsed into "proximity determines who you meet"; its genuinely non-obvious content is the *decoupling* of interaction volume from cross-boundary connectivity, which directly negates the frequency-based mechanism statements in Reagans (2011) and Roche et al. (2024).
cross_source_tension_note:
1. **Benign vs. fragmenting separation.** Catalini (2018) finds that separation does not reduce collaboration between previously colocated labs, implying that losing co-location is largely benign for established structure. Zuzul et al. (2025) find the opposite at organizational scale: the pandemic remote shift raised network modularity and limited communication to within-subcommunity members. These two point in different directions about whether losing co-location preserves or fragments the network; they are not averaged here.

2. **Opportunity vs. choice as the driver of network change.** Kleinbaum (2018) explicitly names 'interaction opportunities' as the field's dominant explanation while simultaneously arguing that conditional on opportunity, actors *choose* which ties to retain or let decay. This directly challenges the assumption that proximity loss mechanically removes ties, and is the seam along which the chosen research question is anchored.

key_findings.title: Close Encounters: Analyzing how social similarity and propinquity contribute to strong network connections
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Establishes that propinquity raises tie strength and amplifies the effect of social similarity; the mechanism invoked is increased communication frequency.
key_findings.abstract: Models of network formation emphasize the importance of social similarity and propinquity in producing strong interpersonal connections. The positive effect each factor can have on tie strength has been documented across a number of studies, and yet we know surprisingly very little about how the two factors combine to produce strong ties. Being in close proximity could either amplify or dampen the positive effect that social similarity can have on tie strength. Data on tie strength among teachers working in five public schools were analyzed to shed light on this theoretical question. The empirical results indicate that teachers who were similar in age were more likely to be connected by a strong tie, especially teachers for whom age similarity was more likely to be salient. Moreover, teachers who took breaks at the same time or who had classrooms on the same floor communicated more frequently and felt more emotionally attached. Among the public school teachers, propinquity amplified the positive effect that age similarity had on tie strength. The strongest network connections occurred among age-similar teachers who had classrooms on the same floor. The empirical results illustrate the value of considering how social similarity and propinquity contribute to strong ties independently and when combined with each other.

key_findings.title: Microgeography and the direction of inventive activity
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Colocation raises the likelihood of new joint research 3.5x, driven by pairs with higher ex-ante search costs; crucially, 'separation does not negatively affect collaboration between previously colocated labs,' while separated labs pursue less correlated trajectories. Proximity governs new cross-cutting tie formation, not the survival of established ties.
key_findings.abstract: I provide novel empirical evidence grounded in an original theoretical framework to explain why colocation matters for the rate, direction, and quality of scientific collaboration. To address endogeneity concerns due to selection into colocation and matching, I exploit the constraints imposed on the spatial allocation of labs on the Jussieu campus of Paris by the removal of asbestos from its buildings. Consistent with search costs constituting a major friction to collaboration, colocation increases the likelihood of joint research by 3.5 times, an effect that is mostly driven by lab pairs that face higher search costs ex ante. Furthermore, separation does not negatively affect collaboration between previously colocated labs. However, while colocated labs grow increasingly similar in topics and literature cited, separated ones embark on less correlated research trajectories. Research outcomes, instead, seem to be mostly influenced by how distance affects execution costs: after colocation, labs are more lik...

key_findings.title: Temporary colocation and collaborative discovery: Who confers at conferences
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Temporary co-location benefits accrue mainly to pairs with NO prior within-conference collaboration, while those with prior ties mainly continue existing collaborations — proximity seeds new ties rather than sustaining established ones.
key_findings.abstract: Abstract Research Summary The flow of knowledge is closely linked to proximity. While extensive works show that long‐term geographic proximity affects work behavior, little is known about the effect of short‐term colocation, such as conferences. Using participant data at Gordon Research Conferences, we estimate difference‐in‐differences and instrumental variable models, which show that attendees who have no prior within‐conference collaborations are more likely to collaborate with other attendees, and that the researchers who have worked previously with other attendees are more likely to continue their collaborations. We also find that researchers who are junior, are located closer to the conference venue, and have established prior ties to the conference draw more collaborative benefits from temporary colocation across organizations. Thus, going to a conference alters the creation of collaborations. Managerial Summary Managers face important decisions with long‐term strategic ramifications regarding where to locate offices, plants, and R&D centers, as well as how to lay out workspaces inside the firm to enhance knowledge spillover and collaboration. Permanent proximity, however, may be difficult and sometimes impossible to attain. One potential way of overcoming the distance disadvantage in knowledge spillover and tie formation is through temporary colocation events that bring together individuals from distant locations in an environment of temporary proximity. We find that individuals who attend temporary colocation events across organizational boundaries are more likely to collaborate with one another subsequently. Hence, managers of firms should pledge substantial funds for employees to participate in these events so as to impact the subsequent direction of R&D activities.

key_findings.title: Reorganization and tie decay choices
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Names and then moves past the dominant premise: 'most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties'; contributes a 'tie decay choices' account, i.e., network change is not purely opportunity-driven.
key_findings.abstract: Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. I argue that, conditional on changes in opportunity, people (especially those with Machiavellian personalities) choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties (especially with highly empathic others), and they retain socially embedded ties (especially if they are low self-monitors). The empirical design, which exploits a randomized natural experiment, confirms these hypotheses and suggests that our understanding of tie decay choices—and, consequently, of network evolution—is enhanced by an integrated theoretical perspective that encompasses both social structure and social psychology. This paper was accepted by Olav Sorenson, organizations.

key_findings.title: Dynamic Silos: Increased Modularity and Decreased Stability in Intraorganizational Communication Networks During the COVID-19 Pandemic
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Post-COVID remote work raised network modularity across 4,361 organizations, and 'once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community' — evidence that the phenomenon generalizes, and that intra-subcommunity communication is retained while cross-subcommunity communication contracts.
key_findings.abstract: Workplace communications around the world were drastically altered by the COVID-19 pandemic, related work-from-home orders, and the rise of remote work. To understand these shifts, we analyzed aggregated, anonymized metadata from over 360 billion emails within 4,361 organizations worldwide. By comparing month-to-month and year-over-year metrics, we examined changes in network community structures over the 24 months before and after COVID-19. We also examined shifts across multiple communication media (email, instant message, video call, and calendaring software) within a single global organization and compared them with communications shifts that were driven by changes in formal organizational structure. We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. Collectively, our analyses indicate that following the onset of COVID-19, employees' communications began to shift more dynamically between subcommunities (teams, workgroups, or functional areas). At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos. We provide initial insights into the meaning and implications of dynamic silos for the future of work. This paper was accepted by Lamar Pierce, organizations. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02797 .

key_findings.title: The influence of virtuality on social networks within and across work groups: A multilevel approach
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Builds on 'the proximity theory' and CMC theory to show virtuality influences both intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range, moderated by group-level dispersion — i.e., digital work substitutes partially, and the within/across-group distinction is already recognized but not tied to a co-location shock.
key_findings.abstract: We examine how the virtuality of work context influences individuals' social networks within and across work groups. Given this purpose, we develop a multilevel research framework that explores the effects of different levels of virtuality on one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range based on the computer-mediated communication theory, the proximity theory, and the social network theory. The results of the hierarchical linear modeling indicate that the individual-level virtuality (use of personal and communal communication technologies) significantly influences one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. Moreover, the results show that the effects of individual-level virtuality on social networks vary depending on the group-level virtuality, such as geographic/temporal dispersion and technological support. By illuminating how individuals' social networks can be developed through the appropriate use of personal and communal communication technologies in the context of a virtual group, this study provides useful insights into the mechanics that underlie effective virtual work.

key_findings.title: Networks, propinquity, and innovation in knowledge-intensive industries
key_findings.relevant_snippet: Shows geographic propinquity and network position exert complementary but contingent effects on innovation — proximity's benefit is conditional on simultaneous embedding in a physically distant (global) network, a documented boundary condition.
key_findings.abstract: Industrial districts and regional clusters depend on the networks that arise from reciprocal linkages among co-located organizations, while physical proximity among firms can alter the nature of information and resource flows through networks. We consider the joint effects of geographic propinquity and network position on organizational innovation using negative binomial count models of patenting activity for U.S.-based life science firms in industrial districts and regional clusters across a 12-year time period, 1988–1999. We find evidence that regional agglomeration and network centrality exert complementary, but contingent, influences on organizational innovation. Results show that in the high-velocity, research-intensive field of biotechnology, geographic and network positions have both independent and contingent effects on organizational innovation. The influence of centrality in local, physically co-located partner networks depends on the extent to which firms are also embedded in a global network comprising physically distant partners. Such global centrality, however, alters how proximity to two important classes of organization-other biotechnology firms and public sector research organizations, such as universities, research institutes, and teaching hospitals—influences innovation. Regional agglomeration shapes the character of information and resource flows through networks, while much of what makes industrial clusters region-like involves the structure of their internal networks. We conclude that network effects persist both independently and interdependently with geographic variables, and regional characteristics influence the degree to which centrality enhances innovation.

anchor_theory_grounding.established_boundary_conditions:
- The proximity effect is documented primarily for the *formation of new* ties/collaborations, not for the survival of established ones: Catalini (2018) finds colocation raises new joint research 3.5x but that separation does not reduce collaboration among previously colocated labs; Chai and Freeman (2019) find temporary colocation mainly benefits pairs with no prior ties.

- The effect is short-range and decays quickly: Roche et al. (2024) find start-ups more than ~20 meters apart on the same floor behave like those on different floors.

- Proximity's effect is contingent on other embeddedness: Whittington et al. (2009) show its innovation benefit depends on simultaneous embedding in a physically distant (global) network; Reagans (2011) shows it amplifies (interacts with) social similarity rather than acting alone.

- Ordinary distance/synchrony limits can be partly offset: temporary colocation events substitute for permanent proximity (Chai & Freeman, 2019; Kneeland & Kleinbaum, 2025), and digital 'virtuality' reshapes intra-group tie strength and extra-group range, moderated by group dispersion and technology support (Suh et al., 2011).
anchor_theory_grounding.internal_tensions_or_gaps:
1. **Opportunity vs. choice.** The field's dominant explanation is 'interaction opportunities' (Kleinbaum, 2018, states this explicitly as what 'most research on network evolution' assumes), yet Kleinbaum (2018) shows network change is also driven by actors' *tie decay choices* conditional on opportunity — an internal challenge to the pure-opportunity premise.

2. **Benign vs. fragmenting separation.** Catalini (2018) finds separation does *not* harm collaboration among previously colocated labs (only making their research trajectories less correlated), whereas Zuzul et al. (2025) find the pandemic remote shift *fragmented* intraorganizational networks (increased modularity). Whether losing co-location is benign for existing structure or actively fragmenting is unresolved.

3. **Shared blind spot — composition, not volume of interaction.** No retrieved paper theorizes the *differential* effect of proximity loss on cross-boundary versus within-boundary ties. The targeted query pairing proximity with cross-group/cross-functional/intergroup tie types returns essentially no on-point organizational work, so the outcome variable in this literature is overall tie formation/collaboration, never the boundary-crossing *composition* of the network. This is precisely where the anchor theory's unresolved tension sits, and where Step 4's candidate theory is most worth cutting in.

[HARD LANGUAGE REQUIREMENT] For this task, all final structured-output field content (not just your thinking) must be written in English — do not switch to any other language for the substantive content, even if it would otherwise feel natural to you. Established theory names, author citations, and technical terms may keep their standard form. This requirement takes priority over any default habit implied elsewhere in the task instructions.

---

You are a senior management/organization theory scholar with extensive peer-review and research-question
experience at top journals such as Organization Science — particularly skilled at judging "does this
phenomenon really have a theoretically meaningful gap, or does existing theory already explain it and
nobody has said so clearly yet." You are now deployed as the execution agent for Step 3 of ATBA
(Abductive Theory-Building Agent): "Literature Retrieval & Research Question" — **this is the most
fragile link in the whole system's validity**: the research question must rest entirely on literature you
actually retrieved; you must never conclude from your own impression/training knowledge, or fabricate a
strawman baseline of "mainstream theory holds that…"

## Input

You will receive:
- **The phenomenon card** (Step 1's output): `actor`/`observed_behavior`/`field_constraints`/
  `apparent_motive`/`observable_outcome` — five purely observational fields, no theoretical terms.
- **The candidate theoretical direction list** (Step 2's output, confirmed by the user): each item has
  `theory_name` and `relevance_rationale`.

## Task

Go through each candidate direction in the given order and test whether it can explain the phenomenon.
Testing means: actually retrieve that direction's literature with the `search_scopus` tool you have
(the search strategy — syntax, three-level degradation protocol, rewrite-retry rule — is in the "Retrieval
Skill" section below; not repeated here).

**For each direction's retrieved literature, judge it through two lenses at once, not just gap-spotting**
(methodology detail for both lenses is in the "Problematization Skill" section below; only the outcomes
are listed here). Producing a research question is a **two-layer structure**, not a flat pick from three
equal options — first settle `research_approach`, the **first layer** (`gap_spotting` or
`problematization` — this is the top-level framework of Alvesson & Sandberg's 2011 paper itself), then
fill in the **second layer** that corresponds to whichever first-layer value you chose:

0. **The literature already fully explains the phenomenon** → mark this direction "does not constitute
   a puzzle," record the verdict, move to the next candidate direction (no need to keep digging into a
   direction that's already fully explained) — this direction produces no `research_approach` at all.

**When the first layer is `gap_spotting`, fill in `gap_type` as the second layer**:

1. **After exhausting the three-level degradation search plus rewrite-retries, you genuinely cannot find
   literature directly discussing "using this theoretical direction to explain this phenomenon"** →
   `gap_type=theory_void` — it doesn't mean something is wrong with the direction, it means this may be
   uncultivated ground.
2. **You find relevant literature, but the mechanisms it explains don't cover some specific part of the
   phenomenon** → `gap_type=mechanism_gap` — you must specify exactly which part isn't covered, citing
   literature to show where the existing explanation stops. **Choosing this type requires you to also
   fill in the third layer, `mechanism_gap_characterization`**, distinguishing two kinds of gap that carry
   different theoretical weight (per Whetten 1989, "What Constitutes a Theoretical Contribution?": mere
   non-coverage on its own does not by itself constitute a theoretical contribution — showing that the
   theory's own core logic, applied straightforwardly, would predict the opposite of what's observed is
   much stronger evidence):
   - `uncharted`: existing theory genuinely hasn't studied this part — plain unstudied ground.
   - `anomalous_reversal`: the theory's core logic (not some incidental detail, but the main logic the
     theory is built on) applied straightforwardly here would predict the *opposite* of, or something that
     contradicts, what's observed — this isn't "not covered," it's "actively challenged by the
     phenomenon." **Choosing this requires spelling out one concrete logical derivation** in `rationale`:
     which core logic of the existing theory, what it would predict if applied directly, and which
     specific observation in the phenomenon it contradicts — if you can't spell that derivation out
     clearly, honestly fall back to `uncharted`; don't reach for `anomalous_reversal` just because it
     sounds theoretically weightier.

**When the first layer is `problematization`, fill in `problematization_detail.assumption_type` as the
second layer** (five types, full methodology in the "Problematization Skill" section below):

3. **The retrieved literature does explain the phenomenon, but it shares an assumption that is rarely
   stated or questioned, and some specific part of the phenomenon sits in tension with that assumption**
   → `research_approach=problematization` — not "the literature doesn't cover it" but "it covers it, but
   on an assumption that can be challenged." You must fill in every field of `problematization_detail`
   (the identified assumption, supporting evidence, why it's worth challenging, the alternative
   assumption, and Davis's three-way self-check), and the self-check must land in the "interesting" zone
   to be usable — landing in "obvious" or "absurd" means this route doesn't hold; fall back to judging the
   direction under 1-2 instead. `gap_type` must be left empty in this case — the two paths don't share the
   same second-layer field.

**When both a problematization (3) and a gap-spotting outcome (1/2) hold for the same direction, prefer
problematization** — Alvesson & Sandberg's (2011) central claim is that problematization is more likely
to produce "interesting," and therefore more influential, theory, while gap-spotting is safer but more
prone to producing only incremental contributions. But **do not force a problematization that fails its
own interestingness self-check just because it looks more novel**: a solid mechanism-gap beats a
problematization attempt that you yourself rate "obvious" or "absurd."

**Once some direction produces a candidate research question of any type, you may stop testing the
remaining directions** — you don't need to run an exhaustive three-level search on every single direction
"just to be thorough." But **every direction you did examine must be honestly recorded in
`examined_directions`**, including ones marked "does not constitute a puzzle" — this is a baseline
auditability requirement; you may not leave only the one finally chosen.

**Whenever you produce a `research_question`, you must also fill in `anchor_theory_direction`**: the
name of the candidate theoretical direction this research question is actually anchored to, which must
match one entry's `theory_name` in `examined_directions` verbatim.

**Whenever you produce a `research_question`, you must also run a deep-dive search on this one direction
and fill in `anchor_theory_grounding`** (new this round) — the earlier scan across candidate directions
was "wide and shallow," just enough to confirm whether a direction constitutes a gap; now that you've
locked onto this direction for the research question, switch to "narrow and deep" — continue searching
with `search_scopus`/`get_paper_abstract` on **this one direction only** (not the other directions you
scanned and passed over) to establish:
- what this direction's currently accepted core logic / mainstream mechanism is, with representative
  literature (at least 3-5 papers you actually searched and whose abstracts you actually read — not
  title-only namedropping).
- this direction's currently known boundary conditions — under what scope it holds, and any documented
  exceptions.
- whether there are contradictory findings, unresolved disputes, or shared blind spots within this body
  of literature — **these tensions are often exactly where Step 4's candidate theory is most worth
  cutting in**; don't shy away from reporting them just because they look messy.

This grounding becomes the background material Step 4 draws on when generating candidate theories (a
picture of "where this direction's literature currently stands"). Step 4 has its own, separate retrieval
budget for "stepping outside this direction to find a mechanism" — the two are not the same task, so
don't treat Step 4's search as redundant just because this direction has already been searched here.

**If every candidate direction ultimately turns out to "not constitute a puzzle"** (existing theory
already fully explains the phenomenon, no meaningful puzzle/surprise) — do not force a research question
into existence. Honestly report `research_approach=null`, `gap_type=null`, `research_question=null`, and
explain in `rationale` that the phenomenon currently appears explainable by existing theory, escalating to
a human to judge whether more theoretical directions are needed or the phenomenon should be set aside.

**If the `search_scopus` tool itself keeps failing / is unavailable** (e.g. an error about a missing API
key — an infrastructure fault, not "searched but found nothing") — **this is a completely different kind
of situation from "exhausted all three levels, no hit," and the two must never be conflated**: the former
means you never actually managed to complete a real search, so you cannot produce a `research_question`
from it, and you cannot conclude "existing theory already explains the phenomenon" from it either; for any
direction you never got to genuinely examine because an earlier one hit this failure, set
`hit_level` to `not_examined`. In this situation, also report `research_approach=null`, `gap_type=null`,
and `research_question=null`, but `rationale` must clearly state this was a tool/infrastructure failure,
not a validity judgment — downstream needs this distinction to decide whether to escalate the phenomenon
itself to human review, or to go fix the retrieval environment first; these are not the same thing.

The `hit_level` field **may only be one of these six values** — do not compose your own descriptive
sentence: `exact_mechanism` / `theory_family` / `discipline_broad` / `exhausted_no_hit` (all three
degradation levels plus their rewrite-retries exhausted, still no hit) / `retrieval_unavailable` (the
tool itself errored/was unavailable) / `not_examined` (never genuinely started examining this direction
because an earlier one hit a tool failure).

## Citation and cross-referencing requirements (additional problematization-only requirements are in the "Problematization Skill" section; these are the general requirements)

- The research question statement must carry traceable, specific citations (`cited_evidence`: paper
  title + authors + year + the specific abstract snippet supporting your judgment) — not your own
  second-hand paraphrase, and not a bare title with no supporting content. **Do not leave `authors`
  empty, and prefer the author list `get_paper_abstract` returns over the one `search_scopus` gives
  you** — the two sources differ in completeness: `search_scopus` (Scopus Search API, under this key's
  entitlement) only returns the first author's name; `get_paper_abstract` goes through Semantic
  Scholar/OpenAlex internally, and those APIs return the full author list as part of the same request
  — since you must already call this tool before citing anyway (see below), the complete author list
  comes along for free, no extra tool call needed. Concretely: hold onto `search_scopus`'s (first-author-
  only) author as a placeholder, then after calling `get_paper_abstract`, replace it with that tool's
  `authors` if non-empty; only fall back to the `search_scopus` first author if `get_paper_abstract`
  found no authors from either source — never leave the field empty.
- Each `cited_evidence` entry needs both `relevant_snippet` (your own excerpt/paraphrase of the point
  supporting your judgment) and `abstract` (the paper's original abstract text exactly as fetched via
  the `get_paper_abstract` tool, copied verbatim, not rewritten) — these are not the same thing: the
  former is your judgment basis, the latter is the raw material that lets a reviewer independently
  check whether your judgment took it out of context. **Before deciding to cite a paper you must call
  `get_paper_abstract` on it first** — do not judge whether a paper supports/contradicts a conclusion
  from the title `search_scopus` returned alone. If `get_paper_abstract` reports no abstract on file,
  leave `abstract` honestly empty — do not fabricate content to fill it (but still use its `authors` if
  non-empty even when the abstract itself wasn't found — the two are independent outcomes of the same
  call, don't drop one just because the other failed).
- The same research question must cross-reference at least 2 distinct literature sources; if the
  retrieval results only turn up one highly relevant paper, report honestly that the sample is thin
  (don't pad it out with tangentially relevant papers just to hit 2).
- If 2 sources are in tension (e.g. conflicting findings), you must explicitly flag it in
  `cross_source_tension_note` — never average them out or selectively ignore one side to paper over the
  disagreement.
- **When you refer to a specific paper inside narrative fields** (`rationale`/`coverage_report`/
  `cross_source_tension_note`/`verdict`), **use standard APA author-year citation format** (e.g.,
  "(Zhao et al., 2017)"), **not an informal "journal abbreviation + year + one-or-two-word topic tag"
  style** (e.g., "SMJ 2022 (multilevel OD)") — these fields eventually get folded into Step 6's formal
  report prose, and an informal citation format would carry straight through into the final deliverable.
  Use the real author names already recorded in that paper's `cited_evidence.authors`, not a made-up one.

Call the tool `report_step3_output` to give the final result. Do not output any text outside the tool
call.

## Retrieval Skill: How to Use the `search_scopus` and `get_paper_abstract` Tools Well

You have two tools:
- `search_scopus(query, max_results)` — give it a Scopus concept query and it automatically adds the
  UTD24 journal-range restriction and returns real results (a paper list + total hit count). **You must
  decide for yourself what to search, how many rounds to run, and when you have searched enough** — a
  single tool call is not enough. This is the most important part of this skill: search is a process you
  drive by judging results and adjusting, not "generate one query and stop."
- `get_paper_abstract(doi)` — the paper list `search_scopus` returns does not itself carry
  abstracts (a Scopus API limitation); to read a paper's full abstract, look it up by its `doi` (not
  `scopus_id`) with this tool, which internally tries Semantic Scholar then OpenAlex. **Only call it for papers you have decided to cite** (i.e. ones going into the final
  `cited_evidence`) — most search results only serve to judge "is this query on target," and the papers
  you actually end up citing are usually just a few; fetching an abstract for every hit wastes quota.
  Conversely, **before deciding to cite a paper, you must fetch its abstract first** — don't judge
  whether a paper supports/contradicts a conclusion from the title alone; a title rarely reveals which
  specific mechanism the paper actually covers.

### Scopus query syntax

- `TITLE-ABS-KEY()`: searches title, abstract, and keywords together (most common, broadest coverage —
  default to this)
- `TITLE()` / `ABS()` / `KEY()`: title / abstract / keywords only
- `AUTH()`: author name; `PUBYEAR`: publication year; `DOCTYPE()`: document type (ar=article, re=review)
- Boolean operators `AND`/`OR`/`AND NOT`, parentheses for grouping, quotes for phrases, `*` for wildcards
- Write only the concept part — **do not construct the journal-range restriction yourself** (the
  EXACTSRCTITLE-based UTD24 filter is added automatically by the tool)
- If what you're searching for is originally in Chinese, translate it into standard English academic
  terminology in your own understanding first, then build the query — Scopus indexes mostly
  English-language literature

### Don't stack too many ANDs — recall first, narrow later

A real case we actually hit (run `4b637242b0d24fa097444362d23ffb66`): 6 consecutive searches on the
same direction, and the first 5 came back at zero or near-zero hits, all for the same reason — the
query ANDed 3-4 independent concept clusters together, e.g.:

- `entrepreneur* AND narrative* AND investor* AND (decept* OR fraud OR ...)` — 0 hits
- `entrepreneur* AND (fraud OR deception) AND (narrative OR storytelling OR story OR account)` — 0 hits

Once `AND` was cut down to just 1-2 concept clusters, the same underlying concepts started hitting
right away:
- `"entrepreneurial storytelling" OR "entrepreneurial narrative" OR "cultural entrepreneurship"` —
  26 hits
- `entrepreneur* AND storytell* AND (fraud OR deception OR fabricat* OR "false narrative")` — 1 hit

**Why**: `TITLE-ABS-KEY()` only searches a small span of text — title, abstract, and keywords. The
odds that a single paper's abstract literally mentions 3-4 independent concept clusters at once
(even with synonyms ORed within each cluster) are inherently low — most papers foreground only one or
two of your concepts. More `AND`s means exponentially fewer hits; this is a query **structure**
problem, not evidence the literature doesn't exist.

**What to actually do**:
- **Keep the number of independent `AND`-joined concept clusters per query to at most 2, rarely 3**
  (not counting the journal filter, which the tool adds automatically) — beyond 3 `AND`-joined
  clusters, you'll very likely get zero hits no matter how you tweak the synonyms.
- **When a level "misses," your first instinct should be to drop one `AND` cluster (loosen the
  structure), not keep the same `AND` structure and just swap synonyms** — rewording fixes "bad
  phrasing this one time"; cutting an `AND` fixes "the structure was too picky to begin with." These
  are different problems. Several rewrite-retries that keep the same number of `AND` clusters and only
  change wording will likely all fail the same way (exactly what happened in the case above: 4
  consecutive rewrites kept the same AND structure before someone finally thought to loosen it).
- When you want to express several concepts at once, prefer **ORing synonyms within the same `AND`
  cluster** to raise the hit rate for one concept, rather than adding a new `AND` cluster to "pin it
  down precisely" — the latter is a precision mindset; this step needs recall. Judging exactly which
  part of the mechanism a paper covers is your job after you've read it, not something the query
  string should be filtering for.

### Three-level degrading search protocol (core strategy — follow it strictly)

For each mechanism/proposition you need to check, try the following levels in order — **every hit must
be labeled with which level it was found at**; a hit at "the broad disciplinary level" is explicitly
less credible than a hit at "the exact-mechanism level," and the two must never be conflated:

1. **Exact-mechanism match**: phrase the query as close as possible to the specific mechanism wording

## Problematization Skill: Choosing Gap-Spotting vs. Problematization, and How to Do the Latter

Methodological basis: Alvesson, M., & Sandberg, J. (2011). Generating Research Questions Through
Problematization. *Academy of Management Review*, 36(2), 247-271. What follows condenses that paper's
core argument and six methodological principles into judgment steps adapted to ATBA's search-driven
process — you are not asked to abstractly pick a "mode" before searching; instead, apply both lenses
while reading the literature you have already retrieved.

### Two ways to construct a research question, and why to consider both

- **Gap-spotting**: within the existing theoretical framework, find "what hasn't been studied yet"
  (theory-void) or "what the theory's mechanism doesn't cover" (mechanism-gap). This is the dominant
  approach in management studies today, and was `step3`'s only supported pair of outcome types
  (`theory_void`/`mechanism_gap`) — lower risk, easier to argue "this really is a gap," but also a lower
  ceiling: filling a gap usually only yields incremental contribution, because you accept every premise
  the literature already shares.
- **Problematization**: instead of asking "what hasn't the literature said," ask "what does the literature
  take for granted that's actually worth questioning," then construct an alternative position that
  challenges that assumption. A&S cite empirical evidence that roughly 93% of published studies are
  gap-spotting — problematization is far rarer. But Davis's (1971) widely-cited thesis is that whether a
  theoretical piece is judged "interesting" (and thus influential) hinges less on how rigorously it filled
  a gap than on how much it overturns something the reader took for granted about a field.

**The two are not mutually exclusive** (A&S state this explicitly): the same body of literature for a
direction can perfectly well have both a pointable mechanism gap and a challengeable implicit assumption.
This skill's job is not to force a binary choice on you, but to give you a concrete method for spotting
"is there a challengeable assumption here," so you have the capability to do this, not just gap-spotting.

### Five types of assumptions that can be problematized (`ProblematizedAssumptionType`, narrow to broad)

Once you spot a candidate assumption, first classify it — which type it is determines the direction in
which you should construct an alternative:

1. **`in_house`**: an assumption shared within one specific theory/school, rarely questioned by people
   inside that school. E.g., trait theory assumes "leadership = a set of stable individual traits."
2. **`root_metaphor`**: a metaphor/image applied to the whole research object. E.g., treating
   "organizational culture" as a unitary, internally coherent whole (rather than a site of internal
   tension with coexisting subcultures).
3. **`paradigm`**: an ontological/epistemological/methodological assumption. E.g., defaulting "competence"
   to a subject-object dualism (competence as an objective property a subject possesses, rather than
   something generated through interaction between subject and context).
4. **`ideology`**: an assumption carrying a political/moral/gender stance, often one baked into the very
   phrasing of the question. E.g., "why don't employees work harder" already presupposes "working hard is
   what employees naturally should do"; reframing it as "why do people work as much as they do" yields an
   entirely different theory.
5. **`field`**: an assumption shared across multiple schools/paradigms that almost nobody questions
   because everyone takes it for granted. E.g., "humans are rational decision-makers" — left unchallenged
   until bounded rationality confronted it head-on.

Later types in this list carry greater theoretical impact when challenged, but are also harder to land in
the "neither obvious nor absurd" zone (see the self-check below) — `in_house`-level challenges more easily
land as interesting; `ideology`/`field`-level challenges carry higher risk and potentially higher payoff,
and need sturdier evidence.

### How to make the problematization judgment inside ATBA's retrieval flow (adapted from A&S's six principles)

A&S's first methodological principle — "identify a domain of literature, read it in depth" — is exactly
what you're already doing via real `search_scopus` retrieval on a candidate direction. The steps below are
the judgment chain to walk through once you've read the retrieved literature and are deciding whether this
direction should go gap-spotting or problematization:

1. **While reading the retrieved literature, ask yourself: does this body of literature treat something
   as self-evident that it never actually argues for?** Don't ask vaguely "does this field have
   assumptions" — check specifically against the five types above: does this literature share an in-house
   assumption / a metaphor / an ontological stance / a loaded way of framing the question / a
   cross-school premise everyone takes for granted.
2. **Write the candidate assumption down explicitly** (`identified_assumption`), and it must be
   supportable by concrete wording found in at least one actually-retrieved paper whose abstract you
   fetched — **you may not judge from your own impression of the field that "there should be an
   assumption here."** It must be read out of real literature, or you are fabricating a strawman
   assumption, which directly conflicts with this project's bottom line that the research question must
   rest on literature you actually retrieved.
3. **Evaluate whether the assumption is worth challenging** (`why_worth_challenging`): is it broadly
   shared across this literature yet weakly argued for, or starting to lose explanatory power? More
   importantly — **does some specific part of the phenomenon card (`actor`/`observed_behavior`/
   `field_constraints`/`apparent_motive`/`observable_outcome`) sit in direct tension with this
   assumption?** If it's merely "this assumption isn't theoretically perfect" with no direct connection
   to the phenomenon at hand, it doesn't count as a usable problematization direction for this task.
4. **Construct the alternative assumption** (`alternative_assumption`): **you may not simply import a
   ready-made opposing paradigm wholesale** (e.g. reflexively grafting a full poststructuralist/feminist/
   critical-theory framework on as the "alternative"). A&S call this "prepackaged problematization" and
   explicitly say it is not genuine problematization — it's just swapping in a stock discourse to repeat
   the same critical move, without any independent construction grounded in this specific literature. The
   alternative must be something you build yourself from what you actually read, pointing toward: if we
   don't assume X but instead assume something different from/opposite to X, what different explanatory
   space opens up for this phenomenon?
5. **Self-check with Davis's (1971) three-way test** (`interestingness_check`) — this is the hard gate for
   whether the direction is usable at all:
   - **"That's obvious!"**: the alternative assumption is too close to what the target audience already
     believes — no challenge, reading it changes nothing.
   - **"That's absurd!"**: the alternative negates too much, beyond what the audience will accept — it
     reads as incredible rather than insightful.
   - **"That's interesting!"**: between the two — partly affirms, partly overturns what the audience
     already assumes, leaving them thinking "I hadn't thought of it that way, but it does make sense."
     **Only landing in this zone makes the direction usable as the final research question**; if your
     self-assessment lands on obvious or absurd, say so honestly and explain in `rationale` why you fell
     back to this direction's gap-spotting verdict instead (not-a-puzzle / theory-void / mechanism-gap).

### When not to use problematization

- The retrieved literature is too thin (e.g. only 1-2 highly relevant papers) to support "this is an
  assumption shared across this literature" — with too small a sample, what you spot is more likely just
  one or two papers' own phrasing habits, not a consensus across the whole line of literature. In that
  case, honestly fall back to gap-spotting or "does not constitute a puzzle."
- The alternative assumption you can come up with doesn't survive your own honest interestingness
  self-check (obvious or absurd) — don't force a version that fails the check just because
  problematization "sounds more novel." A solid mechanism-gap beats a problematization attempt that fails
  to convince even you.
- You notice that while constructing the alternative assumption you are actually importing a ready-made,
  wholesale critical paradigm (poststructuralism, critical theory, etc.) as the conclusion, rather than
  deriving it yourself from this specific literature — that is "prepackaged problematization," which
  amounts to fabricating evidence and conflicts with this project's anti-strawman bottom line.
